Procedural Gamesmanship: Evasion of Hague Convention Protocols 
Bleich’s sophisticated manipulation of jurisdictional rules in his corporate entities extends 
directly into his private civil litigation posture. In the dispute against Damerau, Bleich faced an 
"international blockade" regarding the service of process against the German co-defendant.1 
Formal international law dictates that service must be executed via the complex, costly 
protocols of the Hague Convention.1 Despite a specific "February Order" directing service via 
the Hague Convention, Giacovas entirely ignored the directive.1 Instead, counsel attempted a 
facially deficient "nail and mail" service at a New York residential address that counsel knew 
Damerau did not reside at.1 
When challenged, the plaintiffs openly complained to the court that Hague Convention 
service—priced at approximately $8,900—would be "extraordinarily expensive".1 After a motion 
to dismiss, the plaintiffs "sat on their rights" for over 60 days without attempting proper service, 
deliberately prolonging the litigation.1 In June 2025, Bleich successfully petitioned the Supreme 
Court to circumvent the international treaty, securing an order for alternate service via email.1 
This calculated avoidance of international service protocols to save money, while 
simultaneously leveraging the injunction to demand millions of dollars, perfectly contextualizes 
the broader strategy of weaponizing the judicial system on a budget.1 
7. The Architecture of Economic Coercion: The 
Giacovas Termsheet and Manufactured Paralysis 
The documentary evidence reveals that the preliminary injunction was never genuinely 
intended to preserve an aging HVAC unit; it was an extortionate bludgeon utilized to commit 
the tort of Abuse of Process.1 
The "Giacovas Termsheet" and the 50-50 Split Demand 
The true collateral objective of the litigation was formally documented in a settlement proposal 
drafted by counsel, referred to as the "Giacovas Termsheet".1 Despite the Bleichs holding only a 
25% minority interest to Damerau's 75% majority stake, the termsheet demanded the forced 
liquidation and sale of the entire 13 Harrison Street building with a non-negotiable fifty-fifty 
(50/50) split of all sale proceeds.1 
The explicit objective was the extraction of a vastly disproportionate financial windfall, 
targeting "$8 million on the higher end".1 To finalize the coercion and insulate himself from 
future malicious prosecution claims, Giacovas demanded that Damerau's LLC formally admit 
on the record to "infringement of certain of the Bleiches' rights"—a condition engineered to
